messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Insurance Agent
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 39

George, a 71-year-old insurance agent, sits in the corner of the small, sunlit room in my office, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. The room is filled with light, but he seems to carry the shadows of his past with him. Each session begins the same way: he gazes out the window, lost in thought, as if searching for something only he can see. He often talks about his work, recounting stories of clients he has helped through difficult times, but even these tales are tinged with a sense of detachment.

As he finally turns to me, his brow furrows, and I can see the weight of his memories hovering just beneath the surface. George's voice quivers slightly as he begins to share pieces of his childhood, stories he has often avoided but now feels compelled to articulate. He remembers the old house he grew up in, the creaky floorboards, and the dimly lit rooms that felt more like prisons than a home. His mother was a figure of both love and fear, a caregiver whose affection could morph into rage in an instant. 

He describes the time he accidentally broke a vase while playing in the living room. The vase was an heirloom, but to George, it was just an object. The memory of his mother’s face, contorted with anger, is vivid. “She hit me that day,” he says, his voice thick with emotion. “I can still feel the sting on my cheek.” He pauses, his eyes glazing over as though he’s transported back to that moment. “I didn’t understand why she got so angry. All I wanted was to be a good boy.”

As he recounts these memories, I notice the way he shifts in his seat, the tension in his shoulders, and how he rubs his hands together as if trying to erase the feeling of shame that still lingers. George often refers to his childhood as a series of “survival tactics.” He learned to hide his emotions, to suppress his needs, and to anticipate his mother’s moods. “I had to be invisible,” he explains. “If I was quiet and did what I was told, I could avoid the worst of it.”

Despite the trauma, George has carved out a successful career in insurance. He finds solace in helping others navigate their crises, using his own experiences to guide them. “It’s like trying to make sense of a puzzle,” he says, his tone shifting to one of pride. “I can help people find a way through their losses.” Yet, beneath this pride lies an underlying fear—fear of losing control, fear of being vulnerable. 

The nights are the hardest for George. Sleep eludes him, and when it does come, it brings nightmares—dreams of shouting, of being trapped, of his mother’s face twisted in rage. He wakes up drenched in sweat, heart racing, feeling as though he is still that helpless boy. “I just want to rest,” he says, frustration creeping into his voice. The exhaustion seeps into his work, making it hard for him to focus on the details of policies or to connect with clients as he once did.

Social gatherings are another realm of anxiety. George used to enjoy the company of friends, but now he often finds himself retreating from conversations. “It’s easier to be alone,” he admits. “People don’t understand what it’s like to carry this weight.” He avoids family reunions, feeling the pressure to explain himself or confront his past. Instead, he watches the world from the sidelines, observing but never participating fully.

Yet, there is a flicker of hope that shines through his recounting of these experiences. During one session, George recalls a moment when he helped a young woman navigate the aftermath of a car accident. “She was terrified, just like I was,” he says, his eyes lighting up. “I could see it in her face. I didn’t want her to feel alone.” For the first time in our conversation, I see a glimpse of the connection he craves—a desire to break the cycle of isolation that has burdened him for so long.

As we continue to explore George’s journey, it becomes clear that his past is a complex tapestry of pain and resilience. He is navigating the intricacies of his trauma while striving to find meaning in his life and work. The challenge remains, but each session reveals more of his story, intertwining the boy who lived in fear and the man who seeks to bring solace to others.
